span.p:
MatchingDecision - persisted
every candidate, every sub-score, the weights
version, the solver, and how long it took

div.style: color: rgb(74, 56, 0) !important; display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 200px; text-align: center; width: 200px;

span.p:
why urgency MULTIPLIES rather than adds.
Pure best-fit starves people: a caller nobody is
a great match for waits forever while better-matched
callers overtake them. The multiplier means waiting
itself eventually wins - wait_pressure climbs toward
the 3.0 ceiling and dominates the matrix.
Past MAX_WAIT_BEFORE_ANY_AGENT_S the guard returns
FALLBACK, which removes DEFER and the hot-spot check.
It does NOT re-pick the agent: the solver choice stands.
None of this ran until B12 - waiting_s was frozen
at admit time, so wait_pressure was pinned at 0.

div.style: color: rgb(74, 56, 0) !important; display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 200px; text-align: center; width: 200px;

span.p:
why global rather than greedy - MEASURED (D49).
scripts/run_matching.py --compare scores both on the
same matrix. Across seven seeds greedy left between
0.0% and 8.2% on the table. So the honest claim is not
'greedy is bad' - it is that greedy is usually fine and
occasionally much worse, and it is worst exactly when
agents are scarce relative to skill diversity, which is
when routing matters most.

div.style: color: rgb(74, 56, 0) !important; display: table; white-space: break-spaces; line-height: 1.5; max-width: 200px; text-align: center; width: 200px;

span.p:
why persist every candidate (D18). 'Why did I get
this call?' has to be answerable. A matching decision
you cannot explain is one nobody will trust enough
to leave switched on.
